notes: Sprinkler timer guide series (owner GO 2026-09-05; scope in docs/irrigation-controller-guide-scope.md). Hub-only informational posts that teach a lawn customer to run the irrigation controller on their own wall, one brand per post. GLOBAL RULES, all briefs: (1) informational lane only — no near-me or transactional phrasing anywhere; (2) MANUAL-FIRST: the primary how-to is running the controller BY HAND, following the customer's weekly Waves watering plan for that week. THE PLAN IS AUTHORITATIVE FOR CADENCE AND THE GUIDE NEVER HARDCODES ONE: the plan decides how many runs that week (it can be more than one on a two-day permission), which permitted days they fall on, whether to skip entirely, and — when it asks the reader to check the rain — whether to skip an INDIVIDUAL run. So write "follow this week's plan" and "each run it asks for", never "once a week", and cover all three cases the plan can present: run, skip the week, and check the rain before each run and skip just that one — OFF is the resting position between runs ONLY where every zone is manual — OFF disables all zones, so in a mixed yard whose beds or drip still run automatically the controller stays in its normal run position and the grass zones are separated out instead; wherever OFF is recommended, this qualification must appear with it; a programmed schedule is the optional section at the END of the post; (3) every controller mechanic (dial positions, button names, manual-run steps, rain delay, sensor bypass) must match the cited manufacturer manual — if the manual does not support a step, OMIT it; never invent a button. Where a manufacturer blocks automated requests and no manual can be fetched (Hunter), the owner-reviewed Waves brand guide named in that brief's sources is the authority instead, and no control it does not describe may be introduced; (4) NEVER state a number of allowed watering days per week, an assigned weekday, or allowed hours — watering-day rules come from the customer's county and the current water-shortage order and change; say 'your assigned day and your county's allowed hours' and point to the county; (5) a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one for those rules — say so; (6) Waves does NOT repair irrigation: if a zone will not run, a head is broken, or the box faults, the reader is referred to an irrigation contractor — never imply Waves services, installs, or repairs sprinklers; (7) never describe any product or application as 'safe'; never state prices or dollar amounts — for controller pricing say 'check current pricing'; (8) no manufacturer imagery or scraped photos: hero and body images are generated or Waves-owned, and no manual text is reproduced — link the official manual instead; (9) the weekly Waves watering plan may be mentioned only as 'the weekly watering plan Waves lawn customers receive' — never promise it names the day, never state how many runs it will ask for, and never imply it always asks for the same number; (10) internal links: the lawn treatment prep page and the overwatering-vs-underwatering post at minimum. (11) every post links one lawn care city service page (/lawn-care-{city}-fl/) in the body — the quality gate's hub-link hard check requires it.

briefs.thesis: Rain Bird's dial controllers (ESP-TM2, ESP-Me/Me3) are among the timers we most often find on Southwest Florida homes and the easiest of the big brands to run by hand — which is all most homeowners need: one weekly manual run with the minutes from their watering plan when the plan says to water, the dial back on OFF between runs where every zone is manual, and the programmed schedule left for the few who want it. Frame prevalence explicitly as our own field experience; state no market share, ranking or figure, and attribute it to no source.
outline: Quick answer: which Rain Bird you have (where the model name is printed) and the one weekly move — when this week's plan says to water, one hand run with THIS week's minutes; when it says skip, do nothing at all; then back to OFF between runs where every zone is manual (keep the normal run position if beds or drip have their own schedules)

A short history of Rain Bird: founded 1933 in Glendora, California, around Orton Englehart's horizontal-action impact sprinkler; still family-owned; headquartered in Azusa — verified against rainbird.com/about, dates omitted if the page does not state them

The models you will actually find on a Southwest Florida wall: ESP-TM2 (the builder-grade dial box we routinely find on newer homes — field experience only, no "most" and no market-share claim), ESP-Me and ESP-Me3 (expandable, up to 22 zones, LNK2 Wi-Fi option on the Me3), ESP-RZXe (button faceplate, no dial), SST (simple push-button unit) — one paragraph each, what the faceplate looks like, who it suits

Honest review — pros: dial programming is the simplest of the major brands; manual watering is one dial position; Seasonal Adjust is one knob; parts and manuals are everywhere; cons: multiple start-time slots per program hide an inherited builder schedule, and how many slots and programs a model has differs between them — take the count from that model's own manual rather than quoting one number for the range; the OFF position is the only sure resting state; the Wi-Fi module costs extra; the SST has no per-zone flexibility beyond its buttons. Include a ComparisonTable of the four models (dial or buttons, max zones, manual-run control, Wi-Fi option, best for) with NO prices, and an HonestRejection: who should not bother upgrading or programming a schedule at all

How to run it by hand, per model (HowTo, visible numbered steps): ESP-TM2 — MANUAL STATION is a ONE-ZONE operation, so describe it as such; for the whole lawn use the stored-program manual start the linked manual gives (dial to AUTO RUN, select the program, hold the start control until it begins), exactly as the published Waves Rain Bird guide already describes it; ESP-Me/Me3 — dial to Manual Watering, set minutes, press Hold to Start until STARTED, turn the dial to AUTO; RZXe and SST — no manual for either model is cited in this brief, so give NO button sequence for them: describe what the faceplate looks like and send the reader to the Rain Bird support center for that model's own instructions. Mixed yards (grass plus bed or drip zones): store per-zone minutes once and start the grass program by hand, or run grass zones one at a time. After a run, return the dial to OFF the same day ONLY when every zone is manual — if beds or drip still run on their own schedules, leave the dial in its normal run position instead, or OFF disables their watering indefinitely

Why OFF is the resting position, and the one-time check: with the dial on OFF nothing waters (Rain Bird's own manual says so); before the first hand run, step through EVERY start-time slot in EVERY program the model has — the count differs by model, so take it from that model's manual rather than assuming three programs and four slots — and set to OFF only the slots belonging to grass-only programs, so a builder's leftover lawn schedule cannot fire while the dial sits in a run position. In a mixed yard, LEAVE the start times that drive bed or drip programs alone and remove the grass zones from those programs instead; clearing their starts is the same mistake as leaving the dial on OFF

Watering rules: a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one — run it only on your assigned day and inside your county's allowed hours; those come from the county and the current water-shortage order and change, so check the county page; Waves lawn customers get a weekly watering plan with the minutes per zone and whether to skip the week

Want it to run itself? The optional schedule (dial models): DATE/TIME with AM/PM checked twice, one program (A), one start time chosen so the WHOLE cycle — the sum of every enabled zone's run time — both begins and finishes inside the allowed hours, with the other slots OFF, RUN TIMES per zone, RUN DAYS = the assigned day only, dial back to AUTO RUN; A schedule does NOT end the weekly job: it repeats fixed minutes, so tell the reader that when a later weekly plan changes the minutes they must update the stored run times, and when the plan says to SKIP they must suppress that week's run (rain delay, or clearing the grass program's start for that week) rather than letting a stale schedule water through a rain-covered week. If the reader suppresses a scheduled run by clearing the grass program's start time, they must write the old start down and put it back on the next week the plan calls for a run — a cleared start stays cleared, so an unrestored one disables the turf schedule for good. Prefer a mechanism that expires on its own where the model offers one. rain delay (ONLY where every automatic program may pause together — a controller-wide delay also stops bed and drip programs, so in a mixed yard suppress the grass program alone instead) = dial on AUTO RUN, hold the + button, set days remaining (up to 14); leave SEASONAL ADJUST at 100% because a percentage set once scales every later run-time entry. Rain-sensor handling differs between these models — give the control path each model's own linked manual describes, under that model's heading, and do not present one sensor control as if every model had it; note that a hand-started run may ignore the sensor where the manual says so

When the sprinklers will not run: Waves does not repair irrigation — a zone that will not come on, a broken head, or a box fault goes to an irrigation contractor; Waves still tells you what to water and when

FAQ (4–6 questions): where is the model name; does OFF erase my programs (no); why did my sprinklers come on at noon (AM/PM); can I run one zone only; what does Seasonal Adjust do; do I need the Wi-Fi module
sources: Rain Bird's own About / History page for founding facts (founder, year, city, headquarters, family ownership) — cite it in-post; omit any date or fact the page does not state.

The ESP-TM2 and ESP-Me3 user manuals (linked above) for every dial position, button name and manual-watering step; the RZXe and SST sections stay short and point to the Rain Bird support center for their own manuals rather than guessing buttons.
verify_notes: Every controller mechanic must match the linked ESP-TM2 or ESP-Me3 manual: MANUAL STATION is a dial position on the TM2 (there is no 'Manual Watering button' on the TM2); the Me3 uses the Manual Watering dial position plus the Hold to Start button; rain delay is entered from AUTO RUN by holding the + button (holding the start button from AUTO RUN starts a program instead); the SENSOR dial position sets obey/ignore. If unsure, omit the step and point to the manual.
Do not state how many watering days per week are allowed, which weekday, or which hours — anywhere, including the FAQ. Say 'your assigned day and your county's allowed hours'.
Do not claim Waves installs, services, adjusts or repairs irrigation. The referral to an irrigation contractor is mandatory.

History facts (1933, Glendora, Orton Englehart, impact sprinkler, Azusa headquarters, family-owned) must be verified against rainbird.com/about at draft time; any fact the page does not state is omitted, not paraphrased from memory.
No prices for any controller or module; no 'safe' language; no manufacturer photos or reproduced manual text — link the manuals.
Seasonal Adjust must be described as persistent (it scales every later run-time entry) and the advice must be to leave it at 100% when following weekly minutes.

REQUIRED HUB LINK: the post must link the lawn care service page /lawn-care-sarasota-fl/ as a natural in-body anchor (the content quality gate's hub_link_present hard check accepts a /lawn-care-{city}-fl/ page for lawn posts; /contact/ and blog posts do not count).

Allowed hours apply to the WHOLE cycle, not just the start: a multi-zone program started near the end of the window keeps watering past the cutoff. Wherever a start time is chosen, tell the reader to add up the enabled zone run times and start early enough to finish inside the window.

OFF is the resting position ONLY where every zone is manual. Every instruction to return the dial to OFF must carry the mixed-yard caveat — OFF disables bed and drip schedules indefinitely, which is the fastest way for this post to cost a reader their landscaping. Keep AUTO RUN in mixed yards and remove the grass zones or start times from the automatic programs instead.

A SKIP week means the reader does nothing — no manual start, no runtime update. Every ordered weekly sequence must be gated on the plan not saying skip, and the skip behaviour must be stated in the sequence itself, not only mentioned elsewhere in the post.

The optional schedule is gated exactly like the manual routine: stored run times must be refreshed whenever the weekly plan changes the minutes, and a skip week must be suppressed. Never present a programmed schedule as set-and-forget.

Prescribe exact controls ONLY for models whose manual is cited in sources (ESP-TM2 and ESP-Me/Me3). For the RZXe and the SST, describe the faceplate and point to the Rain Bird support center — do not name buttons or give a sequence for a model whose manual is not linked here.

Cadence comes from the weekly plan, never from this post: it may call for one run or more than one, for skipping the week, or for checking the rain before each individual run and skipping only that one. Write every routine as "do what this week's plan says, for each run it asks for". Never say "once a week" and never treat skip as an all-or-nothing week.

Any controller-wide pause (rain delay, SYSTEM OFF, OFF) stops EVERY zone. Wherever one is offered, say so and give mixed-yard readers a grass-program-only alternative — this is the same failure mode as the OFF advice, in a different control.

briefs.thesis: Hunter's dial controllers (X-Core, X2, Pro-C) are the other box we regularly find in Southwest Florida garages, and the one fact that explains most "my sprinklers stopped" calls is that nothing waters unless the dial sits on RUN — so the weekly routine is a stored program A, refreshed with this week's minutes and started by hand when the plan says to water, the dial back on SYSTEM OFF between runs where every zone is manual, and the programmed schedule left for the few who want it. Frame prevalence explicitly as our own field experience; state no market share, ranking or figure.
outline: Quick answer: which Hunter you have (the model name is on the faceplate). For the DIAL models (X-Core, X2, Pro-C), the weekly move is — when this week's plan says to water, set THIS week's minutes under Run Times, dial to RUN, hold the right arrow about two seconds to start program A, then back to SYSTEM OFF when it finishes (only if every zone is manual); when the plan says skip, do nothing at all. Hydrawise (HC / Pro-HC / HPC) has no dial: send those readers straight to the app-and-touchscreen section instead of any dial sequence

The models you will actually find on a Southwest Florida wall: X-Core and X2 (the common builder dial box, rain-sensor slide switch under the dial), Pro-C (larger, expandable with zone modules), Hydrawise HC / Pro-HC / HPC faceplate (no dial — touchscreen plus the Hydrawise app) — one paragraph each, what the faceplate looks like, who it suits
The one thing to know about a Hunter dial: nothing waters unless the dial is on RUN, which is why a box left on SYSTEM OFF looks broken and is not

Honest review — pros: the one-touch manual start is the simplest weekly move of any major brand; the rain-sensor bypass is a labeled slide switch rather than a menu; Pro-C expands with modules; Hydrawise puts real scheduling in an app. Cons: four start-time slots per program and three programs (A/B/C) hide an inherited builder schedule; on the models where the Manual dial position runs a single station, a whole-lawn run has to come from a stored program; Hydrawise needs Wi-Fi and an account. Include a ComparisonTable of the models (dial or app, expandable, manual-run control, rain-sensor control, best for) with NO prices, and an HonestRejection: who should not bother programming a schedule at all

How to run it by hand (HowTo, visible numbered steps), taken from the Waves Hunter guide: the one-time setup (store the current plan's minutes in program A under Run Times; then, in grass-only programs, clear every start-time slot the model provides — leaving untouched any start time that drives a bed or drip program, and removing the grass zones from those programs instead; dial to SYSTEM OFF only if every zone is manual) and then the weekly run — ONLY when this week's plan does not say to skip: FIRST update Run Times for every grass zone to the minutes in THIS week's plan (the weekly plan recalculates them from evapotranspiration, rainfall and carryover, so last week's stored numbers go stale), THEN dial to RUN, hold the right arrow about two seconds for the one-touch start, and return the dial to SYSTEM OFF the same day where every zone is manual. Mixed yards: if beds or drip still need automatic watering, keep those programs, zero the grass zones inside them, leave the dial on RUN, and use Manual One Station for grass instead

Hydrawise owners: run grass zones from the app or touchscreen for the plan’s minutes, schedule beds and drip SEPARATELY according to their own irrigation guidance — do not tell readers those zones need shorter runs than turf; emitter output and plant demand set those durations, and the weekly plan’s minutes are turf-only — and remove grass zones from automatic programs rather than deleting programs other zones still need

Watering rules: a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one — run it only on your assigned day and inside your county's allowed hours; those come from the county and the current water-shortage order and change; Waves lawn customers get a weekly watering plan with the minutes per zone and whether to skip the week

Want it to run itself? The optional schedule (dial models): set the date and time and check AM/PM twice, use ONE grass-only program, a single start time chosen so that the WHOLE cycle — the sum of every enabled zone’s run time — both begins and finishes inside the county’s allowed hours, with the other three slots OFF; minutes per zone under Run Times, Water Days set to the assigned day only, dial back to RUN; A schedule does NOT end the weekly job: it repeats fixed minutes, so tell the reader that when a later weekly plan changes the minutes they must update the stored run times, and when the plan says to SKIP they must suppress that week's run (rain delay, or clearing the grass program's start for that week) rather than letting a stale schedule water through a rain-covered week. If the reader suppresses a scheduled run by clearing the grass program's start time, they must write the old start down and put it back on the next week the plan calls for a run — a cleared start stays cleared, so an unrestored one disables the turf schedule for good. Prefer a mechanism that expires on its own where the model offers one. controller-wide rain delay from SYSTEM OFF — ONLY where every automatic program may pause together, since it stops bed and drip programs too; in a mixed yard suppress the grass program alone instead; leave Seasonal Adjust at 100% because a percentage set once scales every later run-time entry; leave the rain-sensor switch on Active

When the sprinklers will not run: Waves does not repair irrigation — a zone that will not come on, a broken head, or a box fault goes to an irrigation contractor; Waves still tells you what to water and when

FAQ (4–6 questions): where is the model name; does SYSTEM OFF erase my programs; why did my sprinklers come on at noon (AM/PM); can I run one zone only; what does Seasonal Adjust do; what is the slide switch under the dial
